# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–30 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year). 
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street and other districts); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (market town); Pumpernickel (German principality); Ostend (seaside resort); Hampshire (Dobbin's rented country place "the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (appointed administratrix). All other property "muddled away in speculations" into valueless shares.
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Seduction, Integration, and Final State
**Encounter and Manipulation** (Chapters 27–28): At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos Sedley through calculated performance—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, falsely claiming virtuous past. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Revealed true bohemian nature to Max and Fritz (Schoppenhausen students); had falsely advertised Leipzig concert; won money at cards using young Georgy.

**Dobbin's Opposition**: Called her "the little minx"; stormed at Jos over her character. Amelia embraced Becky warmly and flung Dobbin "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance" of her life. **FACT: Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she grew accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**False Narrative**: Becky claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking" by Rawdon's cruelty; bore poverty; driven to demand separation when Rawdon asked her sacrifice fair fame for Marquis of Steyne advancement. Within week, Jos became "sworn slave and frantic admirer." Changed habits—no more torn collars, rouge-pot suspended, spirit-and-water indulged only privately. Praised Dobbin constantly to Emmy, told her she had behaved cruelly toward him, made Georgy write constantly to Major.

**Jos's Enslavement**: Became Rebecca's "entirely slave" on continent. Lived in enormous Brussels hotel; Rebecca occupied adjacent suite, had her carriage, gave entertainments, lived in genteel manner. Tended him through series of illnesses "with a fidelity most admirable." Jos begged Dobbin to visit when Rebecca at soiree, pleaded for companionship.

**Insurance and Death**: Jos effected heavy insurance on life; lawyers informed Dobbin he was raising money to discharge debts. Dobbin procured prolonged leave, went to Brussels alarmed. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle.

**Will Dispute**: All property muddled away; only £2,000 insurance available, split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (appointed administratrix). Insurance company challenged payment as "blackest case," sent commission to Aix. Rebecca dared them to refuse, declared herself object of "infamous conspiracy" pursuing her throughout life. Solicitors Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes triumphed; money paid, character established. **Colonel Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication with Rebecca.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though continues to style herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declined to see her; she receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly hangs about Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party considers her "a most injured woman." Busies herself in works of piety; goes to church never without footman; name in all Charity Lists. Always has stalls at Fancy Fairs. Encountered Amelia, her children, and Colonel Dobbin at one fair; cast down eyes demurely and smiled as they started away.

## Amelia and William Dobbin's Resolution (Chapter 29)
**Becky's Revelation**: At Ostend (where Jos and Emmy went on doctor's advice), Major Loder and Captain Rook made advances on Amelia "filling her with sickening dismay." Amelia sent secret letter to friend across water. Becky revealed George Osborne was "that selfish humbug, that low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." **"The man was weary of you, and would have jilted you, but that Dobbin forced him to keep his word. He made love to me the week after he married you."** Produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot—and served him right!"

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy wept; internal struggle revealed: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Reconciliation and Marriage**: Two mornings later, Amelia insisted on walking Dike with Georgy. English steamer appeared; Georgy spotted Dobbin through telescope. "A lady in a dripping white bonnet and shawl, with her two little hands out before her, went up to him...she had altogether disappeared under the folds of the old cloak, and was kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present at marriage ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again."

**Dobbin's Achievement**: Married Amelia after fifteen years of devoted service. Quit service immediately after marriage. Rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire country place, near Queen's Crawley). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than anything in world—fonder even than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child; Lady Jane and Mrs. Dobbin became great friends.

## Supporting Characters and Developments
- **Glorvina O'Dowd**: Married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General. Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown."
- **George Osborne (son, now grown)**: "Dashing young gentleman"; hunted and shot with Rawdon; entered same college at Cambridge; quarrelled with Rawdon over Lady Jane's daughter.
- **Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.** (young baronet, Sir Pitt's son): Lives entirely at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane and her daughter; declined to see mother Rebecca.

## New Elements: Lady Carbury Narrative (Chapters 29–30)
**Character and Motivations**: Lady Carbury declares she was cruelly slandered and ill-treated; her statements about herself substantially true. Devoted to her children, especially one. Ready to work her nails off to advance their interests. Has declared object in literary work was to provide for children's needs.

**False Methods, True Desperation**: Her letters to editors detestably false; entire system for achieving success abominably foul, far from honour and honesty. Yet desperation genuine. Conviction that success comes not by producing good books but by inducing critics to say books are good. No ambition to write good book; painfully anxious to write one critics would praise. Had Mr. Broune told her book was trash but undertaken violent praise in "Breakfast Table," his opinion would likely not have wounded her vanity. **"The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was."**

**Welbeck Street House and Activities**: Lives in modest house in Welbeck Street with son and daughter. Made it pretty and pleasant when first took it; proud of comfortable belongings for Tuesday evening literary gatherings. Back drawing-room (divided by permanently closed doors) is her workspace: writes books, contrives system for inveigling editors and critics. Rarely disturbed by daughter; admits no visitors except editors and critics. Son Felix breaks in without remorse.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes; one thing her heart rivetted on. Mother spoilt him as boy and man; even during his folly she hardly ventured to stop him. Almost proud of his vices; delighted in hearing of ruinous extravagance. So indulged he is never ashamed of selfishness in her presence. Philosophy: "carpe diem"—never could see end of anything; never could pass dish he liked in favour of those following. Plays on credit; gets hair cut on credit; formerly had brougham to save cabs.

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance of life has commenced. Cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, head of Carbury branch) passionately in love with her; nearly forty years old. Paul Montague is another gentleman whom Henrietta has seen.

**Secondary Characters Emerging**: Movie Lindson married Ortho Corrett in chapel at Bryngate; couple lives there. Fedette Orlwood complains of aching back. Lubin Brackwood sorts old letters by candlelight in Mirecombe hill farms.
